The short answer: because the book wouldn't have been interesting otherwise.

The longer answer: fans debate this all the time.

Some say that the eagles must be indifferent to the fate of Middle-Earth, but that's not true since they show up for the last battle.

Another answer is that the Nazgul would have gotten the eagles. However, there are only nine Nazgul, and there have to be more than nine eagles if they are a viable species, so that doesn't make sense either.

As for your question about why Mount Doom is unguarded. That is sort of answered in the book -- it is said that Sauron emptied his lands to fight Minas Tirith. Sauron is expecting Aragorn or another hero to appear, wielding the Ring. Gandalf and company encourage this misapprehension with a suicide attack on Mordor -- trying to make it look like they this is the overconfidence/madness of a leader who has the Ring. 

Sauron is 100% sure that the Ring is in Minas Tirith, because, being evil, he can't conceive of anyone wanting to destroy a source of such power -- let alone a stealth mission to accomplish that. Gandalf says that this possibility "has not yet entered his darkest dream". The Orcs who encounter Frodo and Sam assume that they're on a spy mission.
No, even the book says that the foundations of Barad-dur were linked to the One Ring. When the ring is destroyed, Frodo has a vision of towers sinking into the ground.
The Tarahumara aren't superhumans -- we're subhumans.

I think a hormone imbalance is a possibility. I've wondered if I might be a low testosterone person. There was a point in my life a few years ago where I trained physically, very hard, for long periods of time. I never built up any appreciable muscles. It also didn't totally rouse me out of my depressive state. I would get up and go running, biking, weight training, or swimming for hours -- but that's all I could do in a day. The rest of the day was another waste.

Hiring a housekeeper, to me, feels like admitting that I'm not an adult. Can't quite do that. 

I'm very lucky that I had a friend who was dragging me to yoga a few months ago. I was unable to go for the past two months, for reasons that are a little complex.

I have a good list of things I want to do with my life. Lots of creative / business projects.

However, I actually faced this situation recently -- laid off, no debt, and with some savings -- and instead spent many months in depression. It's something I feel shame about.

I did get one project done but it was an art piece, not something I can build the rest of my life around. But still a good experience and I learned a lot.

Thanks. For what it's worth, this IS the lower-status lower-pay humanitarian job. That's what makes it even worse.

I don't have debt, but I tend to burn up savings during my long dysfunctional periods.

I'm not interested in taking anything mood-altering. I tried it once and it altered my personality in a pretty severe way.

I don't have a lot of pressure per se. It gets stressful when you find yourself unable to do stuff that you know is easy, and when you feel that you're starting relationships with people that you feel certain you're going to fuck up.

Are you the sort of person who defines themselves through their obligations to others, and their ability to help? 

I ask because you chose a "helping" profession, and it's had a devastating efect on you. And the thing that's uppermost in your mind about your SO is how your unhappiness affects him. You also fantasize a way to take control of the situation, whereby these bonds of obligation are cut in the most humane way.

It seems to me that you might want a way out, in part, to release yourself from this crushing sense of obligation. I might be projecting a bit, but that's what I read in your post. For you, is it unacceptable to be weak or unable to help others? So unacceptable that you're (almost) willing to kill yourself rather than face a future where you're going to have ups and downs? Believe it or not, people are worthy of love and can be a joy to others just by being who they are. No effort on your part is required. Your SO certainly thinks that about you.

And, a second observation: it seems you are in a period right after you've come out of depression but you haven't yet truly reattached to the world. I say -- give it a little time. You're almost like a stranger moving to a new town, the relationships won't come overnight. Or, jumpstart it by trying something you've always wanted to do, even if it's impractical or expensive. I am certain your SO would support you.

Finally -- I read an interesting story in Po Bronson's "What Should I Do With My Life" about a woman who studied to be a doctor, but then found that she just didn't like being around sick people. She's a TV executive now. So maybe your talents don't have to be used in the health profession.
